Information to generate public support for the war effort. Decades later, 
President Carter used executive orders to implement his agreement with 
the government of Iran for the release of American hostages held since the 
takeover of the U.S. embassy in Tehran. These orders appear as Exec. 
Orders Nos. 12,276-12,285, 46 Fed. Reg. 7913-32 (1981). The Supreme 
Court upheld the legality of President Reagan’s order ratifying and further 
implementing the Carter agreement. The Court rested its conclusions 
partly on the explicit statutory powers of the President and partly, a la 
Justice Frankfurter, on Congress’s implicit authorization for presidential 
initiative in addressing international claims settlement disputes, made 
evident in a history of legislative action ratifying such settlements. Ddiries 
& Moore v, Regan, 453 U.S. 654, 684—686 (1981).
Most executive orders are documents that can fairly be described as 
“internal” to the federal executive establishment and rely most directly on 
the President’s presumed Article II “executive powers” of coordination and 
supervision. Many executive actions, regardless of format, are chiefly 
agenda-setting assignments of work to subordinate administrators 
intended to bear fruit in the months and years ahead, but which have no 
direct iTnmftdiAf.fi pubhc impacts. The limitation of such orders is that one 
president’s supervisory initiatives, born with the stroke of a pen, can be 
undone by another president just as easily. Nonetheless, they may help 
presidents both to mobilize administrative resources for high-priority ends 
and to communicate the Administration’s commitments to the President’s 
campaign promises. Thus, for example. President Trump could not repeal 
the Affordable Care Act, as he had vowed in his 2016 campaign, but he 
could issue an early directive to agencies on 'Minimizing the Economic 
Burden of the Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act Pending Repeal,” 
Exec. Order 13,765, 82 Fed. Reg. 8351 (2017). The order essentially told 
subordinates to exercise their discretion “to the maximum extent permitted 
by law” to administer the law with maximum flexibility.
Likewise, President Biden—presumably recognizing the impossible 
odds for short-term enactment of major new civil rights legislation—could 
still issue as his very first order, “Advancing Racial Equity and Support for 
Underserved Communities Through the Federal Government,” Exec. 
Order 13,985, 86 Fed. Reg. 7009 (1921). The Order assigns to the Director 
of the Office of Management and Budget a variety of tasks to “identify” best 
practices, “consider” recommendations, and “assess” existing policies that 
can affect the equitable distribution of federal government resources. These 
tasks and similar activities assigned to others are intended to yield plans 
to address the order’s objectives. The details of implementation were, 
however, necessarily left for future elaboration. Assignments to “review,” 
“consider,” “assess,” “report,” and the like are also conspicuous elements of 
other Biden orders such as those entitled “Preventing and Combating
